query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a refractory, single‐phase MoNbTaTiV HEA, there exists a critical combination of strain rate and temperature (e.g., high strain rates above ~10⁻¹–10⁰ s⁻¹ at temperatures approaching ~700°C) above which dislocation‐mediated atomic diffusion rapidly enhances grain-boundary nanosegregation, causing a steep, non-linear transition from ductile to brittle behavior that is distinct from conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase MoNbTaTiV refractory HEA produced by powder metallurgy, featuring a refined and homogeneous grain structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the mechanical testing parameters by applying a matrix of strain rates (from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ up to high rates) and temperatures (from room temperature up to ~700°C) to delineate the critical regime.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests (tensile or compressive) conducted in an inert atmosphere across a controlled matrix of strain rates and temperatures representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A threshold accumulation of segregated principal elements at GBs due to intensified dislocation activity.
generation.mechanism: Below the critical regime, modest dislocation activity results in minimal GB segregation, allowing ductile, transgranular deformation. Once the strain rate and temperature exceed a certain threshold, dislocation‐mediated (pipe) diffusion accelerates sharply, leading to a non‐linear increase in GB segregation that drastically reduces GB cohesion and triggers a transition to brittle, intergranular failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A distinct, non‐linear transition will be observed: under low strain rate/temperature conditions the alloy deforms ductilely, while above the critical regime (e.g., strain rates >~10⁻¹ s⁻¹ at ~700°C) there will be a sharp drop in ductility (exceeding a 25% reduction) accompanied by a pronounced increase in grain-boundary segregation measured by APT and a shift to brittle failure modes.
generation.baseline: Mechanical behavior under low strain rate/temperature conditions where minimal GB segregation occurs and ductile, transgranular fracture prevails.
generation.boundary: Testing parameters spanning strain rates from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 10⁰ s⁻¹ and temperatures from room temperature to ~700°C in an inert atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold values may vary with slight differences in composition and processing history. Although slight sample-to-sample variability is possible, the overall predicted steep transition should be reproducible. This hypothesis does not address mechanisms for maintaining ductility beyond the threshold but focuses on delineating the critical regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of mechanical tests on MoNbTaTiV HEA specimens across a systematic range of strain rates and temperatures. Use atom probe tomography (APT) to quantify GB segregation levels and employ SEM/TEM to assess fracture modes, correlating these measurements with the observed ductility.
measurements: Precise strain rate and temperature records for each test
APT quantification of GB elemental segregation
SEM/TEM analysis of fracture surfaces to distinguish intergranular vs. transgranular failure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the transition from ductile to brittle behavior is gradual rather than steep, or if no clear threshold in GB segregation correlates with a sudden reduction in ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV RHEAs were obtained via MA, spark plasma sintering, and hot deformation at various high temperatures and strain rates. With grain refinement and lattice strain increase, the large and inhomogeneous milled powder became refined and homogeneous after the MA. The component elements were segregated under relatively low temperatures and high strain rates. The fluctuation of element concentration occurred only near grain boundaries. The segregation gradually disappeared with the increase in deformation temperature and decrease in strain rate. The interaction between multi-principal elements and dislocation movement was responsible for component element segregation and determined the microhardness variations.

During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

papers.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Powder metallurgy synthesis (mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering) followed by hot deformation experiments under varied temperature and strain rate conditions to track element redistribution.
papers.findings: Grain boundary segregation of certain components is observed at relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates; as temperature increases and strain rate decreases, the segregation diminishes. Such segregation correlates with changes in microhardness.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation generation and movement during plastic deformation create a stress field that drives selected elements (especially those with lower melting points or weak bonding) to diffuse and segregate at grain boundaries.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures with microstructural characterization via atom probe tomography on both single-phase and engineered dual-phase (with preexisting Cr-rich sigma precipitates) alloys.
papers.findings: In single-phase HEAs, fast nanosegregation of principal elements (Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries correlates with intergranular crack initiation and ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (around 500–700°C). The engineered dual-phase alloy, containing Cr-rich precipitates, effectively absorbs the embrittling elements, mitigating ductility loss.
papers.mechanism: Rapid segregation (nanoclustering) of principal elements at grain boundaries reduces cohesion, leading to brittle behavior. Engineering GB segregation through precipitate formation shifts element accumulation away from critical boundaries.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) with enamel-like microstructure featuring engineered nanoscale BCC and FCC phases
papers.approach: Microstructure design inspired by biological enamel, introducing stabilized phase boundaries to enable trans-phase dislocation migration; mechanical testing to validate strength–ductility enhancement.
papers.findings: Stabilization of phase boundaries reduces strain localization, allowing higher uniform plastic deformation. The strategy yields ultra-high tensile strength and good ductility, overcoming issues of localized hardening in nanoscale microstructures.
papers.mechanism: Stabilized phase boundaries act as interfaces that both deflect and dissipate cracks and dislocation pileups, promoting distributed plasticity rather than localized failure.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy with modified (serrated) grain boundary morphology
papers.approach: Heat treatment adjustments (e.g., slower cooling) to induce serrated rather than straight grain boundaries; tensile and creep testing at room and elevated temperatures (650°C) with microstructural and strain mapping analyses.
papers.findings: Serrated grain boundaries help distribute strain more evenly and significantly improve ductility and creep life (with tensile fracture strain and rupture life improvements by factors of ~3.5 and 400, respectively) as compared to alloys with straight grain boundaries.
papers.mechanism: Undulated (serrated) grain boundaries reduce local strain concentration, delaying intergranular decohesion and crack propagation at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with a minor boron addition
papers.approach: Alloy design incorporating a small quantity of boron to induce intergranular boride (likely (Hf, Zr)B2) precipitation; comparative mechanical testing to assess work hardenability and ductility.
papers.findings: The addition of boron leads to intergranular precipitation of borides that markedly raise the hardness and cohesion of grain boundaries, resulting in improved work hardenability and a shift in failure mode from predominantly intergranular to transgranular fracture.
papers.mechanism: Boride precipitates at grain boundaries act to enhance cohesion and impede crack initiation along the boundary, counteracting the embrittling effect that arises from elemental segregation.

established: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness is strongly linked with grain boundary segregation and the formation of deleterious intermetallic precipitates.
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) display unique microstructures that often suppress rapid grain coarsening and intermetallic formation while offering favorable strength–ductility combinations.
However, even single-phase HEAs can experience ductility loss and brittle behavior at intermediate temperatures, suggesting mechanisms beyond conventional intergranular precipitation.

approaches_tried.approach: Inducing controlled grain boundary segregation through deformation (via manipulation of temperature and strain rate) in RHEAs.
approaches_tried.outcome: Observed segregation at low temperatures/high strain rates, with potential impacts on microhardness; indicates reversible segregation behavior dependent on processing conditions.

approaches_tried.approach: Engineering GB segregation by introducing preexisting Cr-rich precipitates to redirect fast segregation away from critical GBs in CrMnFeCoNi HEA.
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully mitigated ductility loss at intermediate temperatures by reducing deleterious GB nanoclustering.

approaches_tried.approach: Microstructure modification via heat treatment to achieve serrated grain boundaries.
approaches_tried.outcome: Serrated GBs effectively distributed strain and increased both tensile ductility and creep rupture life at elevated temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Introducing boron to precipitate intergranular borides and improve GB cohesion in a RHEA.
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced work hardenability and ductility, with a shift from intergranular to transgranular fracture.

mechanisms: Dislocation-driven elemental migration causes fast grain boundary segregation of principal elements, leading to localized reduction of GB cohesion.
Nanoclustering of elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries results in decohesion and early crack initiation at intermediate temperatures.
Stabilized phase boundaries (as in enamel-like microstructures) facilitate trans-boundary dislocation motion and mitigate strain localization.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute strain more uniformly, reducing localized stress concentration at triple junctions and slowing crack propagation.
Intergranular precipitation (e.g., borides) can enhance GB cohesion and inhibit brittle intergranular failure.
disagreements: While conventional understanding assigns toughness loss to deleterious intermetallic precipitation, HEAs in a single-phase state still suffer from ductility loss, suggesting that principal element segregation (rather than trace element precipitation) plays a critical role.
Some studies imply that grain boundary segregation can be manipulated beneficially (via engineering precipitates) whereas others report it as inherently detrimental if not controlled.
open_questions: What is the critical threshold of stress/temperature/deformation conditions that triggers deleterious nanosegregation of principal elements in single-phase HEAs?
How do the kinetics of dislocation-driven segregation in compositionally complex alloys compare quantitatively with conventional alloy systems?
Can a controlled pre-deformation treatment reliably predict or delay the onset of brittle behavior in single-phase HEAs?
opportunities: Design a controlled experimental study comparing an initially single-phase HEA under standard processing with one that incorporates engineered grain boundary features (e.g., preexisting precipitates or induced serration) to distinguish the role of fast segregation.
Utilize in situ high-temperature mechanical testing combined with atom probe tomography to map real-time segregation dynamics at grain boundaries.
Explore hybrid microstructural designs that combine phase boundary stabilization with targeted GB segregation engineering to achieve an optimal balance between strength, ductility, and toughness.
Investigate the effect of deformation rate and temperature systematically in single-phase HEAs to establish mechanistic thresholds for the transition from ductile to brittle behavior.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of dislocation-driven nanosegregation of principal elements at grain boundaries in single‐phase HEAs.
directions.assessment: This approach directly interrogates a mechanism unique to HEAs by correlating dislocation motion with rapid, in situ elemental segregation at grain boundaries. It leverages high-resolution microscopy and atom probe techniques and is strongly supported by prior evidence in RHEAs and fcc HEAs.

directions.direction: Engineer preexisting secondary phase precipitates (e.g., Cr‑rich phases) to redirect deleterious element segregation away from grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: This direction respects the compositionally complex constraint and distinguishes HEA behavior from conventional alloys by using controlled precipitate engineering. Prior studies show that precipitates can absorb segregating elements, improving ductility.

directions.direction: Modify grain boundary morphology (serrated vs. straight) through thermal processing to alter strain localization and segregation kinetics.
directions.assessment: By tailoring the grain boundary features, this approach aims to alleviate local stress concentration and discourage segregation‐induced brittle failure. Published evidence on serrated grain boundaries indicates dramatic improvements in ductility and creep life.

directions.direction: Systematically map the threshold behavior in dislocation-driven segregation under different strain rate and temperature conditions.
directions.assessment: This study distinguishes HEAs from conventional alloys by revealing that a critical combination of strain rate and temperature triggers nanosegregation and brittle behavior. The approach can use controlled tensile tests across a parameter space, with support from prior work on segmentation kinetics.
